studies.title: Artificial intelligence for breast cancer detection in screening mammography in Sweden: a prospective, population-based, paired-reader, non-inferiority study.
studies.design: Prospective population-based paired-reader non-inferiority study
studies.ai_system: Commercial AI mammography reader (not named in the abstract; Lunit is listed among the funders)
studies.humans: Screening radiologists in standard double reading (number not reported in abstract)
studies.finding: The task was detecting breast cancer on screening mammograms in 55 581 women aged 40-74 years at one Stockholm hospital, with screen-detected cancer within 3 months as the primary outcome. A commercial AI reader was tested as a replacement for one radiologist, as a single reader on its own, and as a third reader added to two radiologists. The comparator was standard double reading by two radiologists, and the abstract does not say how many radiologists took part. One radiologist plus AI detected 261 [0·5%] vs 250 [0·4%] cases for two radiologists (relative proportion 1·04 [95% CI 1·00-1·09]), which was non-inferior. AI alone detected 246 [0·4%] vs 250 [0·4%] (relative proportion 0·98 [0·93-1·04]) and two radiologists plus AI detected 269 [0·5%] vs 250 [0·4%] (relative proportion 1·08 [1·04-1·11]), both also non-inferior; the main limitation is that this was a single-centre study counting only screen-detected cancers within 3 months, with no interval-cancer follow-up reported.
studies.limitation: Single-centre study, partly funded by the AI vendor, with the outcome limited to screen-detected cancers within 3 months, so missed and interval cancers are not captured.
studies.check_note: Fixed the garbled AI-alone result to relative proportion 0·98 [0·93-1·04], added the triple-reading CI 1·04-1·11, noted that the abstract does not name the AI product (Lunit appears only as a funder) or the number of radiologists, and restructured the finding.

studies.title: Autonomous Artificial Intelligence vs Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Human Optical Diagnosis of Colorectal Polyps: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
studies.design: Single-centre randomized noninferiority trial
studies.ai_system: CADx (AI-based optical diagnosis system) for colorectal polyps, used autonomously without human input
studies.humans: Endoscopists performing optical diagnosis after seeing the real-time CADx diagnosis (AI-assisted); number of endoscopists not stated in abstract
studies.finding: Patients having elective colonoscopy were randomized so that diminutive polyps were optically diagnosed either by AI alone or by AI-assisted endoscopists, with pathology as the gold standard (467 patients: 238 patients/158 polyps autonomous AI; 229 patients/179 polyps AI-assisted). The AI was a CADx optical diagnosis system working without human input. The comparator was endoscopists who made the diagnosis after seeing the real-time CADx output; the number of endoscopists is not stated in the abstract. Accuracy was 77.2% (95% CI, 69.7-84.7) for autonomous AI vs 72.1% (95% CI, 65.5-78.6) for AI-assisted endoscopists (P = .86), meeting noninferiority, and autonomous AI had higher agreement with pathology-based surveillance intervals (91.5% [95% CI, 86.9-96.1] vs 82.1% [95% CI, 76.5-87.7]; P = .016). The trial ran at a single academic institution and compared AI against AI-assisted rather than unaided endoscopists, and both arms had relatively low accuracy.
studies.limitation: Single academic institution, and the comparator was AI-assisted rather than unaided endoscopists, so it does not show how AI compares with endoscopists working alone.
studies.check_note: Rewrote the finding into the required task–AI–clinicians–results–limitation structure and added patient/polyp numbers and confidence intervals; verdict kept as comparable because the primary accuracy outcome was noninferior, while the surveillance-interval advantage for AI was a secondary outcome.

studies.title: Automated Large Vessel Occlusion Detection Software and Thrombectomy Treatment Times: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial.
studies.design: Cluster randomized stepped-wedge trial at 4 comprehensive stroke centers in one health system
studies.ai_system: Viz.AI cloud-based automated large vessel occlusion (LVO) detection on CT angiography, with mobile alerts, mobile PACS and secure group messaging
studies.humans: Stroke care teams (neurology, radiology, emergency medicine, neurointervention, nursing and others) at 4 comprehensive stroke centers; number of clinicians not stated; 243 patients treated with endovascular thrombectomy
studies.finding: The task was the in-hospital workflow from emergency department arrival to the start of thrombectomy (door-to-groin time) in patients with large vessel occlusion stroke. Viz.AI automated LVO detection with mobile alerts and secure team messaging was switched on at each of 4 stroke centers in randomized order; the number of clinicians was not stated, and 243 patients were included (140 pre-AI, 103 post-AI). Median door-to-groin time was 100 (IQR, 81-116) min before AI and 88 (IQR, 65-110) min after, an adjusted reduction of 11.2 minutes (95% CI, −18.22 to −4.2), and CT-to-groin time fell by 9.8 minutes (95% CI, −16.9 to −2.6); there was no difference in 90-day functional independence (odds ratio, 1.3; 95% CI, 0.42-4.0). The main limitation is that all 4 centers belonged to a single health system with shared workflows and some shared physicians, and the intervention was unblinded.
studies.limitation: All 4 centers belonged to a single health system with shared workflows and some shared physicians, the trial was unblinded, and the outcome was treatment time rather than diagnostic accuracy.
studies.check_note: Named the AI system (Viz.AI), added the pre-AI and post-AI patient counts, the median door-to-groin times and the CT-to-groin confidence interval, and restructured the finding and limitation to cite the single-health-system and unblinded design.

studies.title: Diagnosing Solid Lesions in the Pancreas With Multimodal Artificial Intelligence: A Randomized Crossover Trial.
studies.design: Randomized crossover reader trial (in silico) on a prospective dataset from 2 hospitals in China
studies.ai_system: Multimodal joint-AI model (model 3) combining EUS images and clinical information; image-only EUS-CNN model (model 1) also tested
studies.humans: 12 endoscopists from 9 centers in China: 2 experts, 4 senior, 6 novice
studies.finding: Endoscopists classified solid pancreatic lesions as carcinoma or noncancerous from EUS images and clinical information in 130 prospectively recruited patients, with and without AI predictions, with a 2-week washout between the two arms. The AI was a multimodal joint-AI model combining EUS images and clinical data. Twelve endoscopists (2 experts, 4 senior, 6 novices) took part. On its own the model was more accurate than senior endoscopists (0.92 [95% CI, 0.86-0.96] vs 0.77 [95% CI, 0.68-0.84]; P = .001) and novices (0.69 [95% CI, 0.61-0.76]; P < .001). With AI help, novice accuracy rose from 0.69 (95% CI, 0.61-0.76) to 0.90 (95% CI, 0.83-0.94) (P < .001), but experts (0.88 to 0.82; P > .99) and senior endoscopists (0.77 to 0.80; P = .23) did not benefit; the main limitation is that the trial was in silico, using still images rather than videos, in only 130 patients.
studies.limitation: The crossover trial was run in silico on still EUS images rather than in live procedures, with only 130 patients and 12 endoscopists (with-AI expert results came from 1 endoscopist).
studies.check_note: Changed comparison to 'both' because the paper also compares the AI alone with endoscopists, changed the verdict to mixed because AI help improved novices but not experts or senior endoscopists, corrected the design (the prospective trial used 2 hospitals and the endoscopists came from 9 centers) and rewrote the finding in the required order.

studies.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Colonoscopy Detection of Advanced Neoplasias : A Randomized Trial.
studies.design: Multicenter parallel randomised controlled trial
studies.ai_system: Computer-aided detection (CADe) for colonoscopy; product not named in abstract
studies.humans: Endoscopists in a Spanish colorectal cancer screening program (number not reported in abstract); 3213 persons with a positive fecal immunochemical test randomised
studies.finding: The task was detecting advanced colorectal neoplasia (advanced adenoma and/or advanced serrated polyp) at colonoscopy after a positive fecal immunochemical test. Colonoscopy with computer-aided detection was compared with colonoscopy without it. Endoscopists in a Spanish screening program took part, with 3213 persons randomised; the abstract does not report the number of endoscopists. The advanced colorectal neoplasia detection rate did not differ significantly (34.8% with intervention vs. 34.6% for controls; adjusted risk ratio 1.01 [95% CI, 0.92 to 1.10]), nor did the adenoma detection rate (64.2% vs. 62.0%; aRR 1.06 [99.9% CI, 0.91 to 1.23]), although computer-aided detection increased the mean number of nonpolypoid lesions (0.56 vs. 0.47 per colonoscopy), proximal adenomas (0.94 vs. 0.81) and lesions of 5 mm or smaller. The high adenoma detection rate in the control group may limit generalisability to endoscopists with low detection rates.
studies.limitation: The high adenoma detection rate in the control group may limit the generalizability of the findings to endoscopists with low detection rates.
studies.check_note: Restructured the finding into the required order, added CIs and per-colonoscopy numbers as reported, clarified that the number of endoscopists is not given (3213 persons randomised), and dropped the 'industry funded' claim from the limitation because the abstract only names Medtronic without stating its role.

studies.title: Artificial Intelligence for Real-Time Prediction of the Histology of Colorectal Polyps by General Endoscopists.
studies.design: Prospective multicenter single-group study, 6 US centers
studies.ai_system: CADx (computer-aided diagnosis) for real-time polyp histology prediction
studies.humans: 49 general endoscopists with variable experience in real-time polyp histology prediction
studies.finding: General endoscopists predicted, in real time during routine colonoscopy in 1252 patients, whether colorectal polyps measuring 5 mm or less were adenomas, first without and then with help. They were assisted by a CADx device, which made a diagnosis for 2695 such polyps (96%), and 49 general endoscopists took part. Sensitivity did not differ between unassisted and CADx-assisted predictions (90.7% vs. 90.8%; P = 0.52), while specificity was higher in the CADx-assisted group (59.5% vs. 64.7%; P < 0.001); the share of polyps that could be resected and discarded without pathology was 88.2% assisted vs. 86.1% unassisted (P < 0.001). The authors note that specificity remained suboptimal even with CADx. Because this was a single-group before-and-after design rather than a randomised one, and decision making based on CADx might differ outside a clinical trial, the gains may not carry over to routine practice.
studies.limitation: Single-group before/after design, not randomised, and decision making based on CADx might differ outside a clinical trial; sponsored by Olympus America Corporation.
studies.check_note: Numbers verified against the abstract. The finding was rewritten into the required 3 to 5 sentence structure, adding the resect-and-discard result and the authors' stated limitation.

studies.title: Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making.
studies.design: Retrospective benchmark with reader study on 80 MIMIC-IV cases, all information given upfront
studies.ai_system: Five open-access Llama 2-based 70B LLMs: Llama 2 Chat, OASST, WizardLM (generalist) and Clinical Camel, Meditron (medical)
studies.humans: 4 internal medicine hospitalists with emergency department experience: 3 German doctors in residency (2, 3 and 4 years of experience) and 1 senior US hospitalist (29 years of experience)
studies.finding: The task was to name the primary diagnosis for real emergency patients with acute abdominal pain (appendicitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis or pancreatitis), with the full history, examination, laboratory and imaging findings given upfront, on a subset of 80 cases plus 5 distractor cases. Five open-access Llama 2-based 70B LLMs were tested: Llama 2 Chat, OASST, WizardLM, Clinical Camel and Meditron, each run over 20 seeds. They were compared with 4 hospitalists: 3 German doctors in residency and 1 senior US hospitalist. All five models had significantly lower mean diagnostic accuracy than the doctors (P < 0.001 for each), with a gap in mean performance of 16 to 25 points; the German residents averaged 87.50% ± 3.68% and the US hospitalist 92.50%, and models were especially worse on cholecystitis and diverticulitis, though most matched clinicians on appendicitis. The comparison used only 4 clinicians and 80 cases, and closed models such as GPT-4 could not be tested.
studies.limitation: Only four clinicians and 80 cases were compared, and leading closed models such as GPT-4 were not tested because of MIMIC-IV data-use restrictions.
studies.check_note: Added from the full text the named models, the reader-study design (80 cases, 20 seeds), the 4 hospitalists with their experience, the clinician accuracies (87.50% ± 3.68% and 92.50%), the 16 to 25 point gap and P < 0.001, and replaced the abstract-only limitation.

studies.title: Automation Bias in Mammography: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence BI-RADS Suggestions on Reader Performance.
studies.design: Prospective reader experiment with purported AI giving correct or incorrect BI-RADS suggestions
studies.ai_system: Purported AI system suggesting BI-RADS categories (correct for most cases, deliberately incorrect for 12 of 40 test mammograms)
studies.humans: 27 radiologists (inexperienced, moderately experienced and very experienced)
studies.finding: Radiologists gave BI-RADS assessments for 50 mammograms: a 10-case training set where the AI suggestion was always correct, then a 40-case set where the AI suggested an incorrect BI-RADS category for 12 mammograms. The aid was a purported AI system presented as suggesting BI-RADS categories. 27 radiologists took part, grouped as inexperienced, moderately experienced and very experienced. The percentage of correctly rated mammograms fell when the AI suggestion was incorrect: inexperienced 79.7% ± 11.7 vs 19.8% ± 14.0 (P < .001), moderately experienced 81.3% ± 10.1 vs 24.8% ± 11.6 (P < .001), very experienced 82.3% ± 4.2 vs 45.5% ± 9.1 (P = .003); inexperienced readers followed incorrectly higher AI suggestions more (mean degree of bias 4.0 ± 1.8 vs 2.4 ± 1.5 and 1.2 ± 0.8). The AI was simulated in an experimental setting with a small case set and no unaided reading arm.
studies.limitation: Experimental setting with a simulated (purported) AI on a small case set of 50 mammograms and no unaided control arm.
studies.check_note: Rewrote the finding into the required task/AI/clinicians/results/limitation structure, added the reported SDs, P values and case-set details, and removed 'enriched' from the limitation because the abstract does not describe the case set as enriched.

studies.title: Comparison of Ophthalmologist and Large Language Model Chatbot Responses to Online Patient Eye Care Questions.
studies.design: Cross-sectional masked expert panel evaluation
studies.ai_system: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5), prompt-engineered as 'EyeHelp'
studies.humans: 9 board-certified AAO-affiliated ophthalmologists who wrote the original forum answers; a panel of 8 board-certified ophthalmologists rated the answers
studies.finding: The task was answering 200 detailed patient eye care questions from an online advice forum (Eye Care Forum). The AI was ChatGPT version 3.5, prompted to act as 'EyeHelp' and answer as a human. Its answers were compared with those of 9 board-certified ophthalmologists, with a masked panel of 8 board-certified ophthalmologists rating them. Ratings did not differ significantly between chatbot and ophthalmologist answers for incorrect or inappropriate material (PR, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.77-1.10), likelihood of harm (PR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.67-1.07), extent of harm (PR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.80-1.22) or alignment with medical consensus (P = .35), and raters told AI from human answers with mean accuracy 61.3% (individual range 45% to 74%). The questions came from a single forum and were answered by a small group of volunteer ophthalmologists without patient context, and the answers were judged by ophthalmologists, not patients.
studies.limitation: Questions came from a single online forum and were answered by 9 volunteer ophthalmologists without patient context, which may not represent real doctor-patient care, and answers were judged by a small ophthalmologist panel rather than patients.
studies.check_note: Specified ChatGPT version 3.5 ('EyeHelp' prompt), added the 9 answering ophthalmologists, the missing 95% CIs for harm likelihood and extent, the consensus measure and the rater accuracy range, and restructured the finding and limitation to the required format.

studies.title: Effect of a Computer-Aided Device for Detecting Gastric Neoplasms: A Multicenter, Randomized Controlled Trial.
studies.design: Multicenter randomized controlled trial of AI-assisted vs nonassisted esophagogastroduodenoscopy
studies.ai_system: Computer-aided detection device for gastric neoplasms (name not stated in abstract)
studies.humans: Endoscopists at 24 hospitals in China (number not reported in abstract)
studies.finding: Endoscopists performed upper endoscopy (esophagogastroduodenoscopy) with the aim of detecting gastric neoplasms, and 29,514 patients were randomized to AI-assisted or nonassisted examination. The AI was a computer-aided detection device for gastric neoplasms. The endoscopists worked at 24 hospitals in China; the abstract does not say how many took part. AI did not improve the primary outcome, gastric neoplasm detection after pathological review (1.42 vs 1.25%; RR, 1.13; 0.92-1.38; P = .25); it reduced the number of blind spots from 2.52 to 1.07 (P < .001) and prolonged procedure and inspection time. Detection did improve on original pathology (4.06 vs 3.57%; RR, 1.14; P = .03), and benefit among less experienced endoscopists and during fatigue periods appeared only in exploratory subgroup analyses.
studies.limitation: The primary outcome showed no benefit, the improvement was seen only on original pathology and in exploratory subgroups, and the number and experience of endoscopists are not reported in the abstract.
studies.check_note: Rewrote the finding into the required task/AI/clinicians/results/limitation structure and added the original-pathology result with its numbers; the existing numbers and the verdict were already accurate.

studies.title: Real-Time AI-Assisted Insulin Titration System for Glucose Control in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
studies.design: Multicenter single-blind randomized noninferiority trial in inpatients
studies.ai_system: iNCDSS, an AI-based insulin clinical decision support system giving real-time daily insulin dose recommendations (reviewed and confirmed by ward physicians)
studies.humans: 3 senior board-certified attending endocrinologists with more than 10 years of experience titrated insulin in the control arm; 149 inpatients with type 2 diabetes were randomized (75 iNCDSS, 74 physician)
studies.finding: The task was 5 days of insulin dose titration for inpatients with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes in endocrinology wards at 3 Chinese hospitals. The AI tool was iNCDSS, whose daily recommendations were reviewed by physicians on morning rounds, and 752 of 760 recommendations (98.9%) were adopted. The comparator was titration by 3 senior attending endocrinologists with more than 10 years of experience. Mean time in target range (70-180 mg/dL) on continuous glucose monitoring was 76.4% (16.4%) with iNCDSS and 73.6% (16.8%) with the physicians (difference, 2.7%; 95% CI, −2.7% to 8.0%; P = .33), which met the prespecified −6% noninferiority margin, with no significant differences in hypoglycemic or hyperglycemic events. The trial was short, ran only in Chinese specialist endocrinology wards, and the AI's recommendations were confirmed by physicians rather than applied autonomously.
studies.limitation: The 5-day inpatient trial ran only in Chinese specialist endocrinology wards, and the AI's dose recommendations were reviewed and confirmed by physicians rather than applied autonomously.
studies.check_note: Specified the control arm as 3 senior endocrinologists, added the physician review step and the 98.9% adoption rate, restructured the finding into the required order, and broadened the limitation, while the numbers and the comparable verdict were confirmed.

studies.title: From tool to teammate in a randomized controlled trial of clinician-AI collaborative workflows for diagnosis.
studies.design: Randomised controlled trial using clinical vignettes
studies.ai_system: Custom GPT-4 system, customised only through a system prompt for collaborative diagnostic reasoning, used as a first or second opinion
studies.humans: 70 U.S.-licensed physicians (39 residents, 31 attendings; 97% internal medicine) from several U.S. academic centres; 27 in the AI-as-first-opinion arm, 43 in the AI-as-second-opinion arm
studies.finding: Physicians worked through up to six diagnostic reasoning vignettes, scored on a 19-point rubric. They used a custom GPT-4 system that produced an independent assessment, a synthesis of clinician and AI views, and critiques, either before (first opinion) or after (second opinion) the physician's own assessment. The 70 physicians included 39 residents and 31 attendings; the conventional-resources baseline came from the second-opinion arm's initial answers. Scores were 85% with AI as first opinion (mean difference 9.9%, 95% CI 4.7–15%) and 82% with AI as second opinion (mean difference 6.8%, 95% CI 4.0–9.6%), against 75% with conventional resources; AI alone scored 87% (not significantly different, p = 0.20), reported as 90% in the abstract. The cases were exam-style vignettes, not real patient encounters, and the authors call the trial exploratory.
studies.limitation: An exploratory study using six structured vignettes rather than real encounters, with the conventional-resources baseline taken from the second-opinion arm's own initial answers rather than a separate randomised control group.
studies.check_note: Specified the AI as a prompt-customised GPT-4, added the breakdown of the 70 physicians by arm and training level, noted that the AI-alone score is 87% in the results but 90% in the abstract, explained that the conventional-resources baseline came from the second-opinion arm's initial answers, and replaced the abstract-based limitation with the paper's stated limitations.

studies.title: Care to Explain? AI Explanation Types Differentially Impact Chest Radiograph Diagnostic Performance and Physician Trust in AI.
studies.design: Multicenter prospective randomized study
studies.ai_system: Simulated AI advice with local (feature-based) or global (prototype-based) explanations
studies.humans: 220 physicians: radiologists (task experts) and internal or emergency medicine physicians (task nonexperts)
studies.finding: Physicians read chest radiographs and were then shown simulated AI advice whose correctness and confidence varied, with participants randomised to local (feature-based) or global (prototype-based) AI explanations. Data from 220 radiologists and internal or emergency medicine physicians were analysed. Compared with global explanations, local explanations gave better physician diagnostic accuracy when the AI advice was correct (β = 0.86; Padj < .001) and reduced time spent considering AI advice (β = -0.19; Padj = .01), with an interaction of explanation type, AI confidence and task expertise on accuracy (β = -1.05; Padj = .04). Physicians placed greater simple trust (speed of aligning with AI advice) in local explanations regardless of whether the advice was correct (β = 1.32; Padj = .048), and explanation type did not significantly affect diagnostic confidence or perceived AI usefulness. The AI advice was simulated and there was no unaided reading arm, so the study compares explanation types rather than AI versus no AI.
studies.limitation: The AI advice was simulated and there was no no-AI control arm, so the effect of AI assistance itself versus unaided reading is not measured.
studies.check_note: Added the participant count (220), the Padj values, the interaction and null subjective-measure results, and restructured the finding; retained because the study measures how AI advice and explanation type shape physicians' accuracy and reliance on correct versus incorrect AI advice, though there is no unaided arm.

studies.title: A large language model for complex cardiology care.
studies.design: Randomised controlled trial using retrospective patient data (107 cases)
studies.ai_system: AMIE (Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer), an LLM-based system built on Gemini 2.0 Flash with web search and self-critique
studies.humans: Nine Stanford general cardiologists (two per case, one per arm); three blinded subspecialist cardiologists rated the assessments
studies.finding: General cardiologists assessed 107 real-world cases of suspected genetic cardiomyopathy (triage, diagnosis and management) using text reports and raw test data such as ECGs, echocardiograms and cardiac MRI. In the assisted arm they could read an assessment from AMIE, an LLM built on Gemini 2.0 Flash, and chat with it. Nine general cardiologists took part, with each case done by one cardiologist with AMIE and one without, and three blinded subspecialists judged the paired assessments. Subspecialists preferred AMIE-assisted assessments 46.7% of the time versus 32.7% for cardiologists alone (P = 0.02), with 20.6% ties; assisted responses had fewer clinically significant errors (13.1% versus 24.3%, P = 0.033) and less missing content (17.8% versus 37.4%, P = 0.0021). The main outcome was subspecialist preference on retrospective single-centre cases without history or examination, so effects on real patient outcomes are unknown.
studies.limitation: The primary outcome was subjective subspecialist preference on retrospective single-centre cases without history or examination, so real-world clinical benefit was not shown.
studies.check_note: Results and verdict were correct; I added the cardiologist count and the evaluators to humans, the Gemini 2.0 Flash base to the AI system, restructured the finding into the required order with the tie rate, and replaced the limitation with the paper's own main caveat.

studies.title: Detecting structural heart disease from electrocardiograms using AI.
studies.design: Model development study with retrospective reader study (cardiologists with and without AI) and prospective pilot trial
studies.ai_system: EchoNext deep learning ECG model (convolutional neural network)
studies.humans: 13 board-certified attending cardiologists from Columbia University (3,200 ECG reviews: 1,600 without and 1,600 with AI assistance)
studies.finding: Cardiologists judged whether a patient had structural heart disease (SHD) from a 12-lead ECG plus age, sex and standard ECG measurements, using a set of 150 ECGs with echocardiography-confirmed labels. The AI was EchoNext, a deep learning ECG model, and 13 board-certified cardiologists completed 3,200 reviews, each block first without and then with the EchoNext score. EchoNext alone had an accuracy of 77.3%, sensitivity 72.6% and specificity of 80.7%. Unaided cardiologists had an accuracy of 64.0% (95% CI 61.6–66.4%), sensitivity 61.1% and specificity 66.1%; with AI assistance this improved to 69.2% (95% CI 66.9–71.4%), sensitivity 64.7% and specificity 72.4%, still below the AI alone. The task used only the ECG, without the clinical history, examination or other tests a physician would normally have, and the AI-assisted reads always followed the unaided reads of the same ECGs.
studies.limitation: The task asked cardiologists to detect SHD from the ECG alone, which is not standard clinical practice, using 150 ECGs from one health system with AI-assisted reads always following unaided reads of the same ECGs.
studies.check_note: Added the reported numbers (AI 77.3% accuracy vs cardiologists 64.0% unaided and 69.2% with AI), specified the 13 cardiologists and 3,200 reviews, and changed comparison to 'both' because the paper also tested cardiologists with and without the EchoNext score; the verdict stays ai_ahead because AI alone beat cardiologists with or without help, while AI help also improved them.

studies.title: Assessment of a Large Language Model's Responses to Questions and Cases About Glaucoma and Retina Management.
studies.design: Single-center comparative cross-sectional study with masked Likert ratings
studies.ai_system: GPT-4 (OpenAI, version dated May 12, 2023), prompted as a medical assistant
studies.humans: 15 participants: 12 board-certified, fellowship-trained subspecialists (8 glaucoma, 4 retina) and 3 ophthalmology trainees (2 fellows and a senior resident); 13 participants rated responses
studies.finding: Answering 20 patient questions and managing 20 deidentified cases in glaucoma and retina, with answers rated for accuracy (10-point Likert) and completeness (6-point Likert). GPT-4 was compared with fellowship-trained subspecialists (8 glaucoma, 4 retina), and 3 trainees also took part in the masked rating. Against glaucoma specialists, the combined accuracy mean rank was 506.2 for the chatbot vs 403.4 (P < .001) and completeness 528.3 vs 398.7 (P < .001). Against retina specialists, accuracy was 235.3 vs 216.1 (P = .17) and completeness 258.3 vs 208.7 (P = .005); for case management alone, accuracy did not differ significantly in glaucoma (197.4 vs 190.1, P = .67) or retina (107.6 vs 111.4, P = .70). This was a single-center study at one time point with a small set of questions and cases, rated by the participating clinicians themselves.
studies.limitation: Single-center, single-time-point study with only 40 items, rated on Likert scales by the same small group of participating clinicians rather than independent outcome measures.
studies.check_note: Rewrote the finding into the required structure, added the subspecialty breakdown of participants and the non-significant case-level accuracy results, and sharpened the limitation; the verdict stays mixed because the chatbot was ahead in glaucoma but comparable in retina accuracy.

studies.title: Evaluating LLM-based generative AI tools in emergency triage: A comparative study of ChatGPT Plus, Copilot Pro, and triage nurses.
studies.source: The American journal of emergency medicine
studies.design: Single-center prospective observational study in an urban ED over one week
studies.ai_system: ChatGPT Plus, Copilot Pro
studies.humans: Triage nurses (number not reported in abstract); an emergency medicine physician's ESI assignment served as the reference standard
studies.finding: The task was assigning Emergency Severity Index (ESI) triage levels to adult ED patients, judged against an emergency medicine physician's ESI assignment. ChatGPT and Copilot were given clinical vignettes written by the physician. They were compared with the triage nurses' real-time decisions; the abstract does not report how many nurses or patients took part. Overall triage accuracy was 65.2 % for nurses, 66.5 % for ChatGPT and 61.8 % for Copilot, with agreement with the physician of Cohen's Kappa = 0.537 (ChatGPT), 0.477 (nurses) and 0.472 (Copilot); for high-acuity patients, ChatGPT and Copilot outperformed nurses (87.8 % and 85.7 % versus 32.7 %), and nurses significantly under-triaged (p < 0.05). This was a single-centre, one-week study in which the AI tools worked from physician-written vignettes while nurses assessed patients directly, so the comparison is not like-for-like.
studies.limitation: Single center over one week, with the AI tools given physician-written vignettes rather than the information the nurses gathered at the bedside, and nurses rather than physicians as the human comparators.
studies.check_note: Rewrote the finding into the required structure and added the kappa results; the number of nurses and patients is not given in the abstract, and the abstract's 'no significant difference (p = 0.000)' is internally inconsistent, so it is not reported as a significance claim.

studies.title: Clinical Trial Notifications Triggered by Artificial Intelligence-Detected Cancer Progression: A Randomized Trial.
studies.design: Single-center randomized trial (2:1, patient-level)
studies.ai_system: AI models reading imaging reports to detect cancer progression and predict treatment change, triggering emails to treating physicians with MatchMiner genomically matched trial options
studies.humans: 151 treating physicians (125 at the main academic campus, 26 at community-based network sites) received notifications; 20 707 patients randomized (13 802 intervention, 6905 control)
studies.finding: The task was getting patients with solid tumors onto therapeutic clinical trials when their cancer progressed. When AI models reading imaging reports flagged progression and a likely treatment change, treating physicians were emailed lists of genomically matched trials (MatchMiner); controls got no emails. In total, 20 707 patients were randomized (13 802 intervention, 6905 control), and 2136 emails went to 151 physicians for 1102 patients. Trial enrollment was 2.20% (95% CI, 1.97%-2.46%) with notifications vs 2.03% (95% CI, 1.72%-2.39%) without (difference 0.18 percentage points; P = .41), and consent was 2.96% vs 2.59% (P = .13). The study was at a single academic center, covered only genomically targeted trials, and physician engagement varied (survey response 50.33% per clinician).
studies.limitation: Single-center study limited to genomically targeted trials, with randomization by patient and an outcome (any trial enrollment) shaped by many barriers beyond physician awareness.
studies.check_note: Added the number of notified physicians (151, including 26 at community sites), which the paper reports, removed the incorrect claim that the number was not stated and that all were academic, and expanded the finding to the required structure with consent results.

studies.title: Prospective validation of dermoscopy-based open-source artificial intelligence for melanoma diagnosis (PROVE-AI study).
studies.design: Prospective single-centre observational study with before/after-AI dermatologist assessments
studies.ai_system: ADAE (All Data Are Ext), open-source dermoscopy melanoma algorithm, top-ranked in the 2020 SIIM-ISIC challenge
studies.humans: 11 dermatologists recruiting patients; 5 dominant dermatologists enrolled 97% of lesions
studies.finding: Dermatologists estimated the probability of melanoma in 603 lesions (95 melanomas) scheduled for biopsy, before and after seeing real-time scores from the open-source ADAE dermoscopy algorithm. Eleven dermatologists took part; five enrolled 97% of lesions. ADAE alone had an AUC of 0.857, higher than dermatologists' pre-ADAE estimates (0.780; p = 0.007), and at its prespecified threshold had a sensitivity of 96.8% and a specificity of 37.4%. Dermatologists' AUC improved from 0.7798 to 0.8161 after seeing ADAE (p = 0.042), but their mean calibration worsened (mean predicted probability 20% to 24% against a 16% prevalence; p < 0.001). This was a single-centre, non-randomised study with few dermatologists, and the post-AI management decisions were theoretical because all lesions were biopsied.
studies.limitation: Single-centre, non-randomised before/after design with few dermatologists (one enrolling most lesions), and post-AI management decisions were theoretical because all lesions were biopsied anyway.
studies.check_note: Changed comparison to both because the paper also compares ADAE alone against dermatologists (AUC 0.857 vs 0.780, p = 0.007), added the number of dermatologists (11, of whom 5 enrolled 97% of lesions), noted the worsened calibration, and reworked the finding and limitation.

changes.text: This edition adds 43 studies, including 40 landmark randomised and prospective studies from 2023 to 2026, and rebuilds every section on them: it adds real-patient outcome trials (AI-ECG mortality alerts, liver disease detection, serious illness conversations, stroke workflow) alongside new null trials (AI stethoscope, trial notifications, gastric and colonoscopy detection). It also adds the first evidence on deskilling after AI use, stronger evidence on automation bias, the earlier null GPT-4 vignette trial, and landmark studies on patient-question answers, while noting a new neurology preprint, cardiac MRI and night-shift radiology study.

This edition adds ten studies, including the first randomised trial on real patients outside screening and endoscopy, in inherited retinal disease, a multi-country trial of LLM help on written cases, and new evidence that citations can drive false reliance on AI. It also adds studies on the cost of AI-written care plans, step-by-step diagnosis on simulated cases, ICU outcome prediction, LLM-written discharge summaries, dermoscopy decision support and detection of AI-generated X-rays, which broaden the picture beyond diagnosis while keeping it mixed.

This is the first edition. It covers 11 studies published between November 2025 and August 2026: screening and procedural trials in mammography and colonoscopy, LLM diagnostic trials on vignettes and real emergency department cases, an automation-bias trial, ambient scribes, patient communication and AI-assisted skin diagnosis.

title: AI vs Physician: how AI is changing what physicians can do
summary: The strongest evidence comes from randomised and prospective studies in which clinicians use AI with real patients, and the results depend on the task. In mammography, chest radiograph nodule detection and some ECG-based alerts, AI support found more disease or improved outcomes [S2][S26][S36][S39][S28][S40]. Colonoscopy detection aids tested where endoscopists already found adenomas at high rates [S50][S7], a gastroscopy detection aid [S55], an AI stethoscope [S35] and AI-triggered trial notifications [S63] showed no clear benefit on their main outcomes. On written or simulated cases, large language models (LLMs) often matched or beat physicians and sometimes raised physicians' scores [S30][S31][S33][S57], but not always [S29], and wrong AI advice, and possibly regular AI use, can make clinicians worse [S53][S34][S27].
key_findings: In a randomised trial of more than 100,000 women, AI-supported mammography screening had an interval cancer rate no worse than standard double reading (1.55 vs 1.76 per 1000), after an earlier analysis showed a 44% lower reading workload [S2][S36].

In a pragmatic randomised trial of 15,965 hospitalised patients, an AI-ECG alert to physicians was followed by lower 90-day mortality (3.6% vs 4.3%), mostly in high-risk patients, though how the alert worked is not clear [S28].

Several large randomised trials of AI detection aids found no significant gain on their main outcome, in colonoscopy where adenoma detection was already above 50% or in private practice [S50][S7][S8] and in upper endoscopy [S55], and one observational study found endoscopists' adenoma detection without AI fell from 28.4% to 22.4% after AI was introduced [S27].

On written cases, the first randomised trial of GPT-4 help found no gain for physicians (76% vs 74%) while the model alone scored 92% [S29]; later vignette trials found gains of about 7 to 28 percentage points [S33][S57][S5][S13], with the model alone often still ahead [S5][S9][S57].

Deliberately wrong AI suggestions cut correct mammography ratings sharply, even among very experienced radiologists (82% to 46%) [S53], and systematically biased AI lowered clinicians' accuracy by 11 percentage points, which explanations did not fix [S34][S6].
Less experienced clinicians gain most from AI help [S49][S42][S43], but they also follow wrong AI advice more often [S53][S1].

In blinded ratings of answers to online patient questions, a chatbot was preferred over physicians in 79% of evaluations and rated more empathetic, but its answers were about four times longer and the physician answers came from a public forum, not clinical care [S25].

sections.heading: AI on its own against clinicians
paragraphs: The best head-to-head evidence with real patients comes from narrow, measurable tasks. In a blinded randomised trial of 3,495 echocardiograms at one centre, cardiologists substantially changed the AI's initial ejection fraction less often than the sonographers' (16.8% vs 27.2%) [S32]. In 8,493 emergency patients with suspected heart attack at 18 Korean departments, an AI reading only the ECG separated those with and without myocardial infarction better than the physicians' overall judgement (AUROC 0.878 vs 0.846), though physician judgement was captured as a single 0 to 10 score [S45]. In a single-centre randomised trial, an autonomous AI was non-inferior to AI-assisted endoscopists at judging small polyps (77.2% vs 72.1%), but it was not compared with unaided endoscopists [S47]. In 149 inpatients with type 2 diabetes, AI-recommended insulin doses, almost all confirmed by physicians, kept glucose in range as well as senior endoscrinologists over five days [S56]. As a single mammography reader, AI was non-inferior to two radiologists for screen-detected cancers in one Swedish centre [S46], and in Korea standalone AI found cancers at a similar rate to breast radiologists but recalled more women [S43].

For language models, the picture depends on the material. In a randomised crossover study with patient-actors over text chat, Google's AMIE had higher diagnostic accuracy than 20 primary care physicians and was rated better on most quality measures, though the text-chat format was unfamiliar to the physicians [S30]. Newer reports on curated or simulated cases point the same way [S4][S18][S20], with a neurology preprint scored against autopsy finding the AI comparable to neurologists [S22]. Real-patient comparisons are less favourable: five open-source models were 16 to 25 points less accurate than hospitalists on 80 real abdominal pain cases [S52], and emergency physicians outperformed four commercial LLMs on 180 critically ill patients, although the reference was the physicians' own final diagnosis [S10]. In ICU outcome prediction, AI beat individual clinicians on records but not subspecialists at the bedside, and combining both often worked best [S19]. In emergency triage, chatbots matched nurses overall, but they read physician-written vignettes while nurses saw patients, so the comparison is not like-for-like [S62].

sections.heading: Clinicians working with AI
paragraphs: Randomised trials in real care give mixed but important results. AI-supported mammography screening was non-inferior to double reading on interval cancers in more than 100,000 Swedish women [S2], after an interim analysis showed more cancers detected (6.1 vs 5.1 per 1000, p=0.052) with 44% less reading work [S36]. A large non-randomised German rollout and a Korean prospective cohort also found higher detection with AI [S26][S43]. In a single-centre randomised trial of 10,476 health-check chest radiographs, AI help more than doubled detection of actionable lung nodules (0.59% vs 0.25%) without more false referrals [S39]. AI-ECG alerts were followed by lower 90-day mortality in hospitalised patients [S28] and by twice as many new diagnoses of advanced liver disease in primary care, though uptake was uneven [S40]. Machine learning prompts quadrupled serious illness conversations in high-risk cancer patients and reduced chemotherapy near death, but did not change hospice use [S38]. Automated stroke detection shortened door-to-groin time by about 11 minutes without changing 90-day function [S48].

Other trials found no gain on their main outcome. An AI stethoscope in 205 UK practices did not increase heart failure diagnoses [S35]. AI-triggered emails about matched cancer trials did not raise enrolment [S63]. AI triage for pulmonary embolism halved waiting times for positive scans but did not significantly change radiologist accuracy in a non-randomised study [S44]. Ambient scribes gave mixed results [S3]. Across these studies, benefit seems to depend on whether clinicians act on the AI's output, which some authors point to as a reason for weaker effects [S40][S35].

sections.heading: Reading images and other pattern tasks
paragraphs: Breast screening has the most consistent evidence: one randomised trial with interval cancer follow-up [S2][S36], plus large prospective studies in Germany, Korea and Sweden [S26][S43][S46]. Some caveats: the German study was not randomised and needed statistical adjustment for which exams radiologists chose to read with AI [S26], general radiologists in Korea recalled more women with AI [S43], and the Swedish paired-reader study counted only cancers found within three months [S46].

Endoscopy is less encouraging. Randomised trials in Spain, Germany and a high-detection setting found no significant gain in advanced neoplasia or adenoma detection with computer-aided detection, mostly more small lesions [S50][S7][S8]. A 29,514-patient trial in China found no gain in gastric neoplasm detection, though blind spots fell [S55]. For polyp histology, AI raised specificity modestly in a non-randomised study of 49 general endoscopists [S51]. In skin cancer, dermatologists' accuracy rose with a CNN in a prospective two-centre study with 38 melanomas, and unnecessary excisions fell by 19% [S42]; in another single-centre study accuracy rose slightly but dermatologists overestimated melanoma risk more after seeing the AI [S64]. Online and image-based reader studies show gains on difficult lesions and for primary care physicians [S1][S12].

In other tasks, cardiologists reading ECGs for structural heart disease improved with AI (64.0% to 69.2%) but stayed below the AI alone (77.3%) in a retrospective reader study [S60]. AI-measured ejection fraction on cardiac MRI predicted death marginally better than clinicians' measurements across 27,382 patients [S23]. Nurses and assistants new to ultrasound, guided by AI, produced lung scans of diagnostic quality as often as experts, though no unaided novice arm was tested [S41]. In a small study, AI did not restore residents' chest radiograph accuracy after a night shift, but it did speed reporting in rested readers [S24].

sections.heading: Diagnosis, reasoning and management
paragraphs: On written cases, randomised trials disagree on how much LLM access helps. In 50 US physicians on six vignettes, GPT-4 access did not raise reasoning scores (76% vs 74%), while the model alone scored 92% [S29]. A later trial of 92 physicians on management cases found a 6.5-point gain with GPT-4, with GPT-4 alone scoring about the same as physicians using it [S33]. On 302 published diagnostic puzzles, AMIE raised internists' top-10 accuracy from 36.1% to 51.7%, while AMIE alone reached 59.1% [S31]. A workflow where the AI gave a first or second opinion and critiqued the physician's thinking raised scores from 75% to 82 to 85% [S57]. Newer vignette trials in Pakistan, Kenya, Indonesia, the Netherlands and nephrology found gains of 7 to 28 points [S5][S13][S9], and in several the model alone did better than assisted physicians [S5][S9][S57]. These are written cases, mostly scored with rubrics, not care of real patients.

Closer to practice, general cardiologists given AMIE on 107 real genetic cardiomyopathy cases were preferred by subspecialists more often and made fewer clinically significant errors (13.1% vs 24.3%), though the judging was based on records, not outcomes [S59]. A retinal image tool improved specialists' prediction of the genetic cause of inherited retinal disease in a randomised trial [S16]. In a non-randomised primary care study, patients cared for with an image-plus-language model were more likely to attend eye referral [S37]. Cost is a separate concern: LLM care plans were about three times as costly as treating physicians' plans in a retrospective study [S17].

sections.heading: Communication and documentation
paragraphs: The landmark evidence here is about written answers to patient questions, not consultations. On 195 Reddit questions, blinded health professionals preferred ChatGPT's answers in 78.6% of evaluations and rated them more often empathetic (45.1% vs 4.6%), but the chatbot answers were about four times longer and physician answers came from volunteers on a public forum [S25]. On 200 eye-care forum questions, an ophthalmologist panel found no significant difference in incorrect content or likely harm between ChatGPT and ophthalmologists [S54], a pattern repeated in a later forum study, where ophthalmologists' answers were easier to read [S11]. Against glaucoma specialists GPT-4 was rated more accurate and complete, but for case management it did not differ from glaucoma or retina specialists [S61].

For documentation, evidence is thinner. A randomised trial of two ambient scribes found one cut note-writing time by 9.5% and the other had no significant effect, though both improved a burnout-related score and were used in only about 30% of visits [S3]. Clinicians preferred LLM-written discharge summaries for 95% of 60 long hospital stays, based on ratings rather than any effect on care [S21].

sections.heading: Training, examinations and skill
paragraphs: The register has no studies of AI on medical examinations; the evidence here is about how experience shapes the effect of AI. Less experienced clinicians tend to gain most. On pancreatic ultrasound images, novices' accuracy rose from 0.69 to 0.90 with AI while experts did not benefit [S49]; less experienced dermatologists gained most from a CNN [S42]; general radiologists found more cancers with AI but recalled more women [S43]; and AI-guided novices obtained usable lung ultrasound scans [S41]. The same groups are more exposed to wrong advice: inexperienced radiologists followed incorrect AI ratings more than experts [S53], and medical students relied on wrong AI more than primary care physicians did [S1].

Training to use AI is barely studied. The trial with no gain from GPT-4 gave physicians no training on how to use it [S29], while trials showing large gains in Pakistan gave a 20-hour AI-literacy course [S5]; but that same course did not stop physicians being misled by planted errors [S6]. No study in the register tests whether training itself changes results.

sections.heading: Risks: over-reliance, lost skill and bias
paragraphs: Automation bias is the best-documented risk. When a simulated AI gave wrong mammography ratings, correct ratings fell from about 80% to 20 to 46% depending on experience [S53]. In a randomised vignette study of 457 hospital clinicians, systematically biased AI lowered diagnostic accuracy by 11.3 points, and explanations did not significantly help [S34]. Planted LLM errors cut physicians' accuracy by 14 points [S6], and citations backing wrong answers weakened physicians' resistance to them [S14]. Explanations that make advice easier to follow raised trust whether or not the advice was correct [S58]. One counter-example: primary care physicians barely changed their answers when a dermatology AI was wrong [S1].

Loss of skill now has a first signal. In four Polish centres, adenoma detection in colonoscopies done without AI fell from 28.4% to 22.4% after endoscopists began using AI, though the observational before-after design is open to confounding [S27]. Other unwanted effects include more intensive surveillance and more small lesions found [S7][S50], higher recall among less specialised readers [S43], worse calibration of melanoma risk [S64] and more costly care plans [S17]. On bias across patient groups, the register shows that a model built to perform evenly across skin tones still depended on how clinicians used it [S1], and that clinicians and LLMs struggle to tell AI-generated chest X-rays from real ones [S15].

sections.heading: Where this is heading
paragraphs: This section is interpretation rather than direct evidence. The trials are moving from reader experiments toward randomised studies with patient outcomes, such as interval cancers [S2], mortality [S28] and new diagnoses [S40], and these trials include null results [S35][S63], so claims of benefit can increasingly be tested rather than assumed.

Across vignette studies, the model alone often scores as high as or higher than physicians using it [S29][S33][S5][S9][S57][S60], which points research toward how the work is divided, for example AI as first or second opinion [S57] or AI handling clearly normal cases [S36][S26]. Whether this holds with real patients is unknown, since real-patient diagnostic comparisons remain split [S52][S10][S19]. The repeated findings on automation bias [S53][S34][S6] and the first deskilling signal [S27] suggest that measuring clinicians' performance without AI, and when AI is wrong, will need to be part of future evaluations.

open_questions: Do the gains of LLM assistance seen on written cases carry over to decisions and outcomes for real patients?
Does regular AI use erode clinicians' unaided skill, as one colonoscopy study suggests, and can it be prevented?
Why do some randomised trials with real patients show benefit while others (stethoscope, trial notifications, endoscopy detection) do not: the tool, the outcome, or how clinicians act on alerts?
Does training clinicians to use AI improve results or protect against wrong advice?
Do higher detection rates from AI lead to fewer deaths or to more overdiagnosis and costlier care?
How should work be shared between AI and physicians when the AI alone performs as well as or better than physicians using it?
